title: Metadata: The Envelope
objective: After this level you can explain why who, when and where you communicate can reveal as much as what you said.
summary: Metadata is data about data: for a call, the numbers, times and lengths but not the words. A Stanford study of 823 volunteers showed that pattern alone can reveal a heart condition.

cards.headline: You can learn a lot from an envelope without opening it.
cards.body: Picture a stack of envelopes addressed to one person over several months. You haven't read a single letter, yet you can see who wrote, to whom and when. Is that nothing? Or is it most of the story?

cards.headline: Data about data
cards.body: That outside information has a name: metadata, meaning data about data. For a phone call it's the numbers, the time and how long you talked, but not a word you said. Files carry it too. A file's metadata describes things such as its format, which is how a program knows what kind of data is inside.

mascot.line: People mix these up: metadata isn't the message. It's everything about the message except the words.

cards.headline: 823 volunteers and one heartbeat
cards.body: In a Stanford study published in 2016, researchers collected the call and text logs of 823 volunteers: numbers, times and lengths, no content. One person called a cardiology group, a pharmacy and a hotline for a heart-rhythm monitoring device. From that pattern alone, the researchers inferred the person likely had a cardiac arrhythmia. Nobody listened to a single call.

cards.headline: Why the envelope matters
cards.body: One call says little. Months of them reveal where someone goes, who they are close to and even highly sensitive traits. And locking the message itself doesn't hide the envelope: encryption leaves visible that two people are talking, and when, where and for how long. That's why metadata can matter as much as the words.

cards.headline: Metadata: unpacked
learned: Metadata is data about data: who, when, where, how long
A file's format is metadata too
Call patterns alone revealed a likely heart condition
Encrypting a message doesn't hide its metadata

questions.prompt: Match each metadata idea with its description.
questions.explanation: Metadata is data about data, a Stanford study used the call and text logs of 823 volunteers, and locking the message doesn't hide the envelope.

questions.prompt: How did the Stanford researchers infer a volunteer's heart condition without hearing any calls?

options.label: They asked the volunteer's doctor for records
options.rationale: They used only the call and text logs.

options.label: The pattern of numbers called pointed to heart care
The phone recorded the calls in secret
options.rationale: The logs held no content at all.

options.label: They read the volunteer's text messages
options.rationale: They had the texts' metadata, not their words.

questions.explanation: Calls to a cardiology group, a pharmacy and an arrhythmia-monitor hotline pointed to a likely cardiac arrhythmia.

questions.prompt: Level 10 said a file's format tells a program how to read its bytes. What kind of data is that format label?

options.label: Encrypted data
options.rationale: A format label describes the data; it doesn't lock it.

options.label: Content, like the words in a letter
options.rationale: It describes the content rather than being it.

options.label: A packet header from the internet
options.rationale: Packets aren't what this is about.

questions.explanation: A file's format is metadata: it describes the data inside so a program knows how to read it.
